title: Strategies for Integrating Disparate Social Information
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
description: Participants complete counterbalanced one-peer, three-peer, and four-peer estimation blocks. The visual blocks collect an initial numerosity estimate before social revision; the four-peer block measures aggregation without a personal prior estimate.

included: five-round one-peer visual estimation and revision block
published one-peer species, counts, source pools, and selection algorithm
published fixed species, true-count, and treatment schedule
five rounds per LN, HN, HF, and HC condition plus ten fillers
exact three-peer lookup for every round and every valid initial estimate
published control anchor pools with invalid zero sentinels rejected
all six published block-order permutations assigned cyclically
source-derived instructions and comprehension checks before every block
accuracy points for one randomly selected round per original block
multimodal image input for the first estimate only
excluded: browser sliders and six-second client-side timer
cognitive model fitting and downstream belief-dynamics simulations
original animal sprite artwork referenced through now-unavailable external URLs
implementation_scope.reason: The package reconstructs the complete 40-round three-block behavioral task. Browser motor behavior, wall-clock response timing, post-task questionnaires, and downstream modeling are outside the agent-experiment runtime.

sources.license_note: See source/SOURCE_PROVENANCE.md for per-artifact provenance and the regenerated-stimulus boundary.

findings.main_hypothesis: Peer disagreement reduces social information use: adjustment is larger in low-variance LN than high-variance HN.
With variance held high, participants adjust more when two peers are close to their initial estimate (HC) than when two peers are far from it (HF).
The distribution of peer estimates changes adjustment strategies, especially compromise versus other responses.
Without a personal prior estimate, four-peer control judgments lie closer to the peers' arithmetic mean than main-task revisions.
